children: President Donald Trump has nominated Matthew Zandi, who was chief of staff to the recently departed head of the US Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, for a seat on the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

If confirmed by the US Senate, Zandi would give Republicans a 3-1 edge on the commission, which enforces federal laws banning workplace discrimination and has been central to the Trump administration's efforts to eradicate diversity, equity and inclusion policies.
The White House announced Zandi's nomination late on Monday.

Zandi was chief of staff to Harmeet Dhillon, a close Trump ally who resigned last week after reshaping the Justice Department unit that enforces civil rights laws to pursue administration priorities including voter data requests and the crackdown on DEI.
Zandi could not immediately be reached for comment. The Justice Department and EEOC did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Before joining the DOJ last year, Zandi was a managing director at consulting firm Guidepost Solutions, which conducts risk management, investigations and compliance work, according to his profile on the networking site LinkedIn. He was an assistant US attorney from 2002 to 2006 and has also worked at law firms Nixon Peabody and Kaufman Borgeest & Ryan.

Some civil rights groups immediately criticized the nomination, tying Zandi to various DOJ policies adopted under Dhillon that they said had harmed workers and the public. That included "weaponizing" the federal False Claims Act by threatening government contractors and grant recipients with legal action over their DEI policies, said Lauren Khouri, senior counsel at the National Women's Law Center.
"This nomination seeks to equip [EEOC Chair] Andrea Lucas with total power to execute her radical anti-worker agenda,” Khouri said.

Lucas, a Trump appointee, has moved aggressively to implement the administration's agenda including by launching investigations into diversity programs at major companies, universities and law firms. The commission is also poised to roll back a rule expanding legal protections for pregnant workers and limit the ability of federal employees to pursue administrative cases alleging workplace discrimination.

The Republican-led Senate is scheduled to be in session until December 18. If the Senate fails to act on the nomination, Trump would have to re-submit it next year to a chamber controlled by Democrats, who picked up seven Senate seats in last week's midterm elections.
